blocks.x: Joe Robichaud. Okay, it's going.
Well, this is Joe Robichaud from New Orleans, Louisiana.
Just where were you born?
I was born right here in New Orleans, around St. Mary and Camp, right in Magazine Market.
Or uptown?
Yeah, North Channel.
What was the date you were born?
I was born on March 8th, 1900.
You can just sit back and relax. I'll pick up everything. Can you remember the first music, how you got interested in music? The first music you heard?

Well, I'll tell you how I actually got interested in playing music. I was quite a young kid and I had a piano player that used to call Game Kid. And my mother had a piano in that time, I think it was around about 1907. And I was quite small and he used to come and play the piano. And at that time, all the piano players were very famous around New Orleans at that time. And I kind of liked the piano, but I didn't, I wasn't interested in learning then, but I used to just like to listen. And I met a little fellow that called Cooney. He used to play piano. And every Sunday he used to come up around Santa Anax, Hilda Santa Anax's house. And they used to have parties that I used to go to. And then I got interested in him and I used to go around with him. But I never tried to play at that time. But I loved it, but I didn't play it. I think about learning to play then rather. So in school, they was teaching music. I was attending New Orleans University then. And everybody had to learn a little bit about music.
Was that up on St. Charles Avenue?
That was on St. Charles Avenue.
I took a picture of that once.
Oh, yeah. So anyway, then after I came out of school, I still didn't play the piano. I was great about playing baseball and I become a ball player.
Yeah.
And I went all over playing baseball.
You ever hurt your hands, break any fingers?

No, I hurt a little finger one time. Once I got hit on the knee, but the finger wasn't broken. And the knee was so wild, but it got all right. Then after playing ball and I began to learn, I got interested in the piano and I started to practice the blues. And I had a fellow called Lawrence Cook. He used to live in Arstown. He played very good blues. And I used to go around him and he used to show me how to play the blues.
And I met... Lawrence Cook?
Cook. Yeah.
I wonder, there's a fellow up in New York that made a lot of piano rolls. Would that be the same fellow?

No, no, that's not the same. No, that's not the same. I didn't think so. I wonder. No, it's not the same, Cook. This was... A fellow here, there was a musical family. It was Lawrence Cook, Moona Cook, Minor, Willie. And they had a sister called Julia. And one they called Lee. And all of them played piano.
Oh, the whole time.

All of them played the piano. So I was around their house and then Steve Lewis, he came along and he was a very good pianist. And then I began to... He began to show me things and then from him, I used to go to his house all the time and he taught me. I say he was responsible for as much as I know today about the playing because he was a very good pianist and he used to like me and everything he knew he would show me.
He really showed you then. You didn't just listen to him, he showed you how to...
But he used to show me how to execute things because he, at that time he didn't read, he was playing with P-Ron's band.
Yes, I knew you were playing.

Yeah. He made a couple of piano rolls too and he wrote quite a few tunes. Then I went off with a show, with a tent show. And I was playing in what they call a 49 camp where they dance, you know, it was one of those tent like a diamond dance. Well, I played for that show, it was O.J. Beattie's show. And I played for that show, I went, I was with him about nine months.
What was the name again?
O.J. Beattie. Beattie. Beattie, yeah.
Was it more of a carnival?

That's what it was, a carnival. Carnival. And they had a, what they call a 49 camp, was a dance, you know, where they dance, 10th and 2nd dance. Well, I played for that show for about nine months, then I left, I went to Chicago. And the first band I played with was a follower called Tick Chambers, he was a trumpet player from here.
You played with the Tick?
Tick Chambers, yeah.
In Chicago? In Chicago.
And they had Jimmy Strokes and a follower called Joe, a drummer, those three were from here.
Do you know about what year that was, could you remember?
Yeah, that was in 1918.
Time of the war then.
Yeah, and they had, this right after the war ended.
Yeah.
Yeah. And then they had Eddie Palmer, I think, played with that band.
I appreciate it.
Yeah, Trombone. So anyway.
Oh wait, is that Roy Palmer?

Roy Palmer, I'm not to say, Roy Palmer, not Eddie Palmer, Roy Palmer. So then I came back to New Orleans and I stayed about two months and I joined a show named Washbone and Weaver. And I went out with that show. And I played on shows, Tom Moss, went from Washbone and Weaver to Tom Moss. And I came back to New Orleans and I went out and played with a band they called the Black Eagle. That was E.T. Thomas, trumpet player from Crowley, Louisiana. Well, I played with him about two years. And I married, got married whilst I was playing with him.
Now do you remember who else was in that band? Was Lawrence Dewey?

Lawrence Dewey was playing clarinet. We had a clarinet. We had Robert Gilbert. He was playing a C melody. Then he got an alto after, a little later. And we had a fellow that called Casey on bass. Walter Thomas was the drummer. That was E.Vance's drummer. And we had a guitar player called Kudu. I never did. That's the only name I knew him about was Kudu. He played guitar player. Nice guitar. So then finally...
Was there a trombone fellow by the name of Gus? Did you ever play with him out there?

No, I know him well. Gus Faulkner. I met him. We used to meet him. He had the Banner Band. And the Black Eagle Band and the Banner Band. They were the two best bands around at that time. We used to play in Texas together. We met up all the time.
Did you ever play with Bunk or run across him out there?

Well, I met Bunk. The first time I ever heard Bunk play was in Houston, Texas. I used to hear him talk about Bunk, but I had never heard him play. So one day we were playing an advertisement in a wagon for a dance. And they were on a wagon playing an advertisement for a show, for a theater. And this guy played, oh, played trumpet, you know, jazz. And I said, who is it? I said, who is that trumpet playing? They said, don't you know him? I said, well, no. I never, I don't know him. I said, but he plays, he's a good horn. So the fellow said, he's from New Orleans. I said, that's Bunk Johnson. And I said, well, that's Bunk. They said, yeah, that's Bunk. I said, well, I heard talk of him, but I never did hear him play.
About what year was that?

That was in 1923 or 24. I'm sure it was 1923. And I say, I will say this, that a lot of people who never heard Bunk, when he was a young man, there was so much difference in the Bunk than it is now. Because you could tell about, I mean, before he passed, you could tell that he was a good trumpet player in his young days. But people in him don't notice how much he could play because he was really powerful. He had a wonderful tone and he could execute his horn. He was a very good trumpet player.
He was in good form then when you heard him.

Yeah, when I heard him play, he was actually good. He was really good because I had heard a lot of good trumpet players and all the trumpet players that they were talking about were good during those times. And I don't think they had anybody any better than him, I'll tell you that. Because he really played. And then after I met him then, then I came to New Orleans and played around here quite a while at the Music Box that was at Canal and Crown Lamp. And I played at the La Vida with Lee Collins and David Jones. And I played on Astor and we made some recordings for the Victor at the Italian Hall on Espinade Street. Then finally I had a six-piece band and I played at the Entertainers. From there I went to New York, made some records for the Brunswick, which they put on Vocalium. And from there I formed a 15-piece band with Joan Lunsford, Will Bostic. I had Van Dyke, had Freddie Colman, drummer, Willie O'Connor. I had Jeff, Sam Dutre, Clemens Tivallon, Warren Joseph, which we call Frog. I had Kildee, he passed not long ago. His name was Henry Holloway, he was a very fine trumpet player and arranger. And I had Tukey, a fellow called Tukey, his name was George Girard. And he was a very good trumpet player. And we had Eugene Ware, which was another good trumpet player.
George Girard, is that the white trumpet player?
No, it wasn't white George Girard. This was another...
But the same name, huh?
Same name, yeah.
Svelte the same dude.

Svelte the same, yeah. And this guy was a wonderful trumpet player too. He played very... He's still out there and I think he's in Thibodeau or somewhere around there. But he was a very good trumpet player at that time. So we had... We played a lot of arrangements. And we played with all the big bands. We played with Jimmy Lunsford. We played with Duke Ellington. We played with Count Basie two or three times. We played with Claude Hopkins when he had his band. We played with Andy Quake twice.
Was that mostly around New York when you...

No, we played... On the road. Yeah, we played Birmingham. We played Birmingham with Claude Hopkins. We played Birmingham with Andy Quake. We played New Orleans with Andy Quake. We played New Orleans twice with Count Basie. We played with Jimmy Lunsford. Here they used to call it the Pelican then. And that Beazie used to book bands then. Yeah. We played with Andy Quake... With Jimmy Lunsford.
Somebody go ahead and answer it so I'll just turn it on. You had a band when you played Officer Kirk and...
And at that time they had... Cycloform player. He was very... He was very famous at the time because he... He wrote... Chan of the Weeds.
Don Redman? Don Redman.

Yeah. He had a band. And he had a... He had a fellow... Two men once played with my big band with him at the time. He had Eugene Porter. And he had Earl Bostic. Earl Bostic had left. And went to Ohio. And went to New York. And he got to play...
Where did Earl Bostic come from? He wasn't from here, was he? No.

Earl went to school here. He's from Oklahoma. He's from... Tulsa. He's from Tulsa. A few miles out of Tulsa. He's from Oklahoma. And he came down here. And he was attending Xavier University. Oh, that's right.
I remember.

And then he played around here with Sidney's. Band. And he went on the boat. And then he came back. And then he got to play in my band. And he stayed with me quite a while. And he went to... To Ohio. And he went on a job that he... Our whole band was supposed to go on this job. And Miss... Gwendolyn... Gwendolyn... She promoted this job. And it was in Toledo. And finally, I got the show together for her. And she booked the show. And the show went over there. So we was waiting on a telegram for the band. And we went out on the road. And we was in Galveston, Texas. And four days before the opening, they sent and told them that they wanted the band, that the show was there. And we had four days to get there. So the telegram right away told them it was okay. And they had to send... It was mailing the contracts. And so this telegram came to Galveston. I was living at Margaret's. Lady, her name was Margaret. She had a tea room. And we used to stop there. And her name was Margaret Sherrill. So the telegram came. And another young lady went to the door. And they told them they had a telegram for Joe Robichaux. And she told them that there wasn't nobody there by that name. And so when we got ready to leave, three days afterwards, when we got ready to leave, we was going to Port Arthur. And we were always telling Margaret goodbye. And she said...

And Margaret called my name, and I had a big trailer with the name on it, too, right in front of the house. And she said, oh, is that Joe Rova's show? And Margaret said, yeah, that's Joe Rova. And she said, oh, a telegram come here a couple of days ago, and I told her, man, there was nobody here by that name. So when we called up the telegram office, and they stated, they read the telegram out. And so finally, the same day that I was going to pull off to the plate, that's the same day I was supposed to be in Cleveland. So I got in touch with Miss Wonderland right away, and the man had to hire a band out there. So he had hired the band, had to give the band a two-month contract, I think it was. So now in the band, they were short of a trumpet player and also an alto player. So Herman Franklin was playing in my band, and he had played with these fellas before. And so they were in Herman. So Herman went up there, business was kind of slow with us then, so Herman, he went there. And so when he got up there, and he sent for Oyle Bostic, and Oyle went up there, and Oyle, they played up there quite a while. And then Oyle went to New York. And this Let Me Uptown, we had the same arrangement, we had been playing it with Gene Cooper made. That was his, Oyle's tune. And he went, and they played that number for him, recorded it. And ever since that, well, Oyle did very well, and he's a wealthy man today. So I was glad for him, and I haven't saw him since he left the band. He's been here about six or seven times, and I was playing in the quarters, and I never did get a chance to see him. We had quite a band, if I have to say it myself, during that time. We played all over the United States, and also Cuba.
In Cuba? I didn't know you went to Cuba.
Oh yeah, we went to Cuba with the big band.
How long were you there?
I played, I stayed over there three weeks. I played the theaters. I had the band and a show too.
Is that mostly in Havana?

No, we played Havana, and we played other towns around. And I can't recall any of the towns. I have a scrapbook here with some of the towns. But we played there, we had a big welcome there. And it was a pretty nice trip, and we came back and we played all through Florida, because we had been going to Florida time and time. And then we traveled with the Mills Brothers through Florida and Georgia. They had our band and the Mills Brothers together. And that was successful. And we had a very good singer. Her name was Joan Lunsford. Her right name was Daisy Lowe, but I gave her the name as Joan Lunsford.
And she was a very, very fine singer, and everybody liked her every place she went.

And we had Baby Briscoe. She was a dancer, and she was a great dancer. She danced, I'm telling you, it was a very few men could out dance her. Yeah, she was a very good dancer, and I tell you, everywhere she went, everybody was crazy about her too. And in fact, she was the best woman dancer I ever seen.
What type? Tap dancer? Tap dancer, yeah.

She was one of the best women tap dancers I ever saw, because she could dance, and she danced with both feet, and everything the men could do, she could do it. And then she used to dance and make some sauce and dance, and never lose time. She was a really wonderful dancer. Then I had a trumpet player at one time by the name of Ann Cooper. She was a woman trumpet player. Oh, man. And she was a real good trumpet player.
Come from here?

No, her home is not here. No, her home is not here. I forgot where Ann told me her home was. But she came to New Orleans, and she played with, I think, oh, she was to play in Papa Sutter Stans band. But some way, I don't know if they got together or what. So I got needed a trumpet player, and they told me about them. So they told me that she could, I went and talked to her, and she said she could read a little. She said she wasn't much of a reader. That's what she said. See, so I told her, I said, well, we rehearsed, and we rehearsed things. I said, you don't have to be no sight reader because we rehearsed all the arrangements. So finally I went and got her. We had a rehearsal, and she came up to the rehearsal. Well, she couldn't find out she could read better than what she explained to us, you know. So she read pretty well, and she could hit higher notes than anybody in the band. We had some pretty good trumpet players and pretty powerful. But she used to take her, she could just take her horn up and just hit altissimo C. Just take it up and hit it without, like some trumpet players have to run the scales or something. But she could take it, just pick it right up and just hit the note right now. So we began to give her the parts that had the high, real high notes. I mean, I gave them to her because she was strong, and then she could hit these notes, and she never miss them. She never did miss. She just, we'd have a whistle, and she'd take them things and play them and hit the notes. And she played with me quite a while, about a year and something. So I had decided, we talked, the band talked it over, so we said, well, we're going to take another trumpet player and put in a band, which I had three, and it would be four, and say, let's use Ann for a feature with solos like we was doing with the singers and with Brisco. So I think she misunderstood me when we said that. I think she thought that we were taking her out to put a trumpet player in her place, so she wasn't doing the work. But she was really playing intercession really good. She was fitting there good and a lot better than any men that we had. But we just thought it would be a novelty to have her come out and play different numbers, you know, where she could play real well. And she could play different solos and things that they were featuring. She knew them. She could play them.
What was her last name?
Her name was Ann Cooper.
Cooper.
Cooper, yeah.
Cooper. Cooper.

Cooper. Cooper. And I learned that she was around Chicago, but she left here and she went to Detroit, and I heard that she was in Chicago. Last time I was in Chicago, a fellow told me that she was playing with somebody around Chicago in a loop. And I said, I'd like to see her. I met a piano player there. And I had, his name was Bubba, I forget his name, I've been knowing him, I've been knowing him before I knew how to play. But anyhow, he said she called it. And he told me Ann was playing somewhere in the loop with some fellows in the loop. But she was a good piano player, she was a wonderful trumpet player I wanted to say. And she had a wonderful tune, and she could finger hone, and she used to play on a style like Louis Armstrong. That was her style of playing. And everybody heard her, everybody liked her.
Not very many girls that played good trumpet.

No, playing good trumpet playing like her, because she played just like, you'd never think it was a girl. And one thing about her, they used to have jam sessions during those times, and we used to play places, and when the fellows get off, they used to jam. Like we played Oklahoma City, and the first time we went there, played Oklahoma City, Oscar Moore, he was in Oklahoma City.
Guitar.

The guitar man. Him and they had an alto player there, he got famous too, he was in Oklahoma City. So they invited us out to a place where they had a jam session, they had trumpet players, and they had a couple of white boys there. I think Benny Goodman was in town there. And they all was there playing. And this Ann Cooper, she don't do nothing but just go there and pull out her horn and start the blowing, and see if they stay there until, if they stay there ten hours, she's there ten hours. And she was, and blow along, and blow along. Yeah, she was, everywhere we went at, people was great about her. She'd get into anybody's session. And she was very good. Now and I heard a many good musicians in the States, and I played date and dates with a lot of them, we played a lot of them, we played the bands of music with the best bands that was available during that time. And I made a trip overseas, 58, the last of 58, but we might as well say 59 because of 59 when 60 when I got there. And I heard a many good musicians over in Europe, both England, Denmark, Germany, Sweden. And I always tell, I mean I was glad it was one of the greatest experiences because I was under the impression, I guess like a lot of musicians are, that the fellas over there don't play the type of music that we do. But if anybody's thinking that they're barely mistaken because the boys 16, 17 years old, 15 years old, they're playing jazz. They're crazy about New Orleans music. And they play this music, they got these records, they got records that practically we didn't think that existed. That's right. And we went over there and found these guys with all these old records. They even had a record of Sal Morgan made, about Sammy got the best go here, Bugger Lucy or something, Bugger Lucy Stone. Now they had all those tunes in which I wouldn't have ever thought about them before because some of the fellas that were playing music I knew it well. And I had forgot all about them until these fellas get to call their names when they played the records. They had Joe Oliver's records, the first record he ever made. They had the first colored singer he ever sang on records. And I mean it's amazing to see them have those things. And these young kids, when you go and find them playing Dixieland, it's quite a surprise, which they call New Orleans music. It's quite a surprise to hear these kids, how they play these things and how they got jazz clubs all over England and the majority of them, they're all youngsters. That's the thing which is so amazing. They're teenagers and you go there and they got these jazz clubs and every jazz club we went in, it was packed in jam. Yeah, it was packed in those jazz clubs. And we went to some of the large, we went to two, well it wasn't two large, there was one ahead in Scotland and one ahead in Kent Coyle's club. Now it's a good sized club, I mean it's as big as any club on Boybun Street. But you go in there and you can't get in, there's so many people in these clubs, you just can't get in the door. And we went to Liverpool, we went to a jazz club, the first, we were off that Saturday night. And we went there and heard a band playing, and they had two bands rather playing. They had to make way for us to pass, it was so crowded in there. And these guys, they played some jazz music to you, just think you're right in New Orleans when you hear them play. And then you'd be astonished, you'd have to look and say, well how do these guys play all this music? And then they'd tell you whose style they like and who they, and it really was amazing. And then we went to another jazz club in Liverpool, and it's the only place that I've been to where, we went to where you could stay, you know they could play as long as they want. Because it was in a business session where they had offices, you know nothing but no residents. And they could play all night if they wanted on Saturday. So we went there and we stayed, I stayed there till about, we stayed there till about 4.30 in the morning and left them down there playing.
When you played over in England, did you play mostly for concerts or for dancing or dances, what were they? Like a night club?

Well, most, all our playing was concerts, all except in Denmark. We played concerts in Denmark but in Copenhagen they opened up a club, a jazz club, a new jazz club, followed by the name of Andy, Hendrix, Carl. And we played in this club four nights. Oh yeah. Yeah. But all the rest of it was concerts and television. Now we played television job in Germany. We played one in Denmark. And we were interviewed on a television in England.
Somebody told us that it was going to be over here, but I couldn't find out anything about it.
Well, they said it was going to be over here, but I don't think that, no, I don't think they showed it, no. I don't think, I think somebody, Mr.
understood something. They got it wrong, I think, when it was explained. I don't think it was over here because nobody saw it. So I'm sure it wasn't over here.
You got into Sweden then too for a while. Was it Stockholm?

We played Stockholm, Sweden, and we had so many people at this kind of sector. The fire marshal wouldn't leave anybody else in. And this is one of the largest places that I played in. It had about five balconies to this. That's why they give all these ballets and all the big concerts, different violinists. Like a big opera house. Yeah, that's what it was. And they couldn't get any more people in there. And the fire marshal turned the people away. And I'm telling you, it was amazing, the crowd and the way they accepted this New Orleans jazz. I mean, they inspires you. You know, everywhere we went they had an enthusiastic crowd. And they just clap and they just whistle and they, I don't know, they just make you play for you. They make you think you're doing more than what you are for you. And it actually inspires you to play. And that was everywhere we went at. We never had a dull crowd. We played two places in Sweden. And we played, I think we played everywhere in England you could play. And on top of that we was playing right behind Louis Armstrong. Everywhere we was playing. Louis Armstrong was playing five or six days before we got there. And we didn't have a bad concert. That's one thing I must say. We played in some awful large places and we never had a bad concert on the whole tour.
You got into Scotland you say.
Scotland was wonderful. Here's another thing. I like to say this. The musicians over there, the way that they accept us, the way that these musicians made us feel good.
You're talking about how the musicians made you feel at home.

Yeah. Now the first place, I'd like to start this out. We went into Liverpool. First, before I get to that, I don't want to leave this out. We went into Liverpool. We went on this ship on the corner line. It was the Corinthia. That was the name of the ship, Corinthia. And on this ship, they had two bands on the ship. And the captain, the mate, and the crew, I must say the crew, they made it so pleasant for us on the ship that we didn't have a dull moment on the ship.
How many passengers about on the boat?
Well, on this trip, we must have had about 400 passengers on the ship. Because it wasn't many as it usually had. But we had about 400 passengers on this ship.
Before you went over, somebody said you'd have to dress up in tuxedos for dinner every night. Did you have to do that?

Well, yeah. We dressed up in tuxedos for dinner only. That was only for dinner. Now, for breakfast and lunch, you didn't have to be full. And New Year's Eve night, we was at sea. So, anyway, we said, well, we would play about three or four numbers for the passengers on the ship. Because everybody treated us so nice on the ship. I mean, all of the passengers were so nice.
They all knew you were musicians.

Yeah, they all knew we were musicians. And everybody would talk with us. And even we met a lady and her husband. They were going to Dublin, to Ireland. And they sent us over champagne. And from that on, every night, every time we'd go into lunch, the people would come over and sit down and talk with us. And we'd go up where the band was. They would treat us so nice up in there. They welcomed us. They welcomed us. We just was like we were home. We'd sit at sea. And they had theater on there. We used to go to theater, practice every night. And then when we'd get into Liverpool. And then when we'd get into Liverpool, it was snowing and cold. And here was a band out there and that snow. Cold as it was out there playing, serenading us as the ship was landing. You know, it was one of these Dixieland bands. And they was out there in the snow blowing, you know. And I said, gee man, I said, now you know, cold as it is out there. And it's snowing like that. I said, I know this would be one time I wouldn't be playing for anybody, you know.
Did they have a sign up to know that they were welcoming you or something?

Well, yeah, they was all hollering, George Lewis, you know, and they had signs and they played. So when we got in, when they got to playing, when the ship landed, they came on the ship and it happened to be Chris Barbara and his band. And so anyway, well, that was fine. And we talked with them and we came on off the ship. It'd take a little time, you know, because we came off the ship. So that night we went where these fellows were playing at. And they played real good. So we left there. We left that Sunday and went into London. And when we got to London, the train got in there about 4.30 or something to 5 that evening. And when we get there, they had police. They came back there and they helped us back, you know. And I didn't know what was happening. I said, well, I wonder what's the matter. We, you know, they kept us there about 25, 30 minutes and it was cold out there, you know. So they said, all right, you know, before. So they said, all right, y'all can come on now. And the police, well, we did get to the, to where you go out the station. It looked like Carnival Day out there. And it had so many people and they all was on top of sheds and buildings and the police. They must have had about 25 or 30 police that were trying to get us through the crowd. And they had a brass band out there playing nothing but New Orleans tunes like we play on parades here. And it was Kemp Kaya. They had a brass band about 12, 14 pieces. And they was out there playing all these New Orleans tunes. And these people was clapping and howling. A shed fell in with some people.
And they got hurt.

Yeah, yes. The ambulance taking one or two to the, to the hospital. But I learned that there wasn't, nothing too serious. So I was glad for that. And the ambulance couldn't, the crowd was so, the ambulance couldn't pass by. This was brushing up against the people, moving and blowing to get out, you know. And we had a time getting out there. And I never saw so many photographers before in my life. It looked like they had 200 or more there. And they were taking pictures in the newspapers. And they were always full of the doors. Always full of that next stair and Joyce Lewis and the shed falling in. And well it was a wonderful center. I felt, I really felt good because this band was playing. That's like the New Orleans band's place on the parades here. And it was quite a surprise, you know. To hear them play all those marching tunes and play all these spiritual things. So that night we went out to Ken Kiley's club and they had some, oh it was crowded. You couldn't move in there. Did they have dancing there too? They have dancing, yeah they have dancing. They have dancing in there, but it was so crowded that night nobody couldn't dance because the people could, you couldn't move, you know. So I sat in and played with them, played a couple of pieces. Well everybody sat in a while with the exception of George. And we went to a place they called the, let's see what they call that, it's a little, the cottage they called it. The cottage. But we went there and they had a jam session there. Well they had all kinds of musicians. They had modern and jazz musicians and then we all sit and we played there until time for that, from the Stop the Music thing. Then I went out and played with this fellow, his name is Alan Yates. And they had a wonderful band. They had a real good band. They had a clarinet player there. He was a wonderful clarinet player there. Then they had a vibraphone player there. He was a subtle man. But man, that man could play some vibraphones. He could play vibraphones and he was so happy with playing. It was good for me to look at him play. And I sat there and I played with them quite a while and I went about 15 miles out and I sat in with another band. I don't know the name of the band. I don't know the name of the band, but the fellow, his name was Rudy Marcellus. He's from New Orleans. And he's kin to this Marcellus who's got this tourist code up here. And his cousins are very, very wonderful pianist. And he plays tenor, alto, clarinet, bass, and all the instruments he plays, all the instruments, real good. He's a good musician. And he told me that's his cousin. So anyway, I sit there and played with them. And now he's playing guitar and singing the blues. And when they left here he didn't play anything. He said he learned it since he'd been in England. He said he went over there with a ballet show. And he stayed over there. Then I met up and we played four concerts with Ken Kaya's band. And I think we played three with Chris Barber's band. And with Chris Barber's band they came over here in the swap.
They may still be here. I don't know.

Yeah, they may because they told me they was coming to New Orleans. They were coming here to see me. And they asked me where you were and I gave them your address. And they said they were coming by to see you.
And we haven't heard from them here yet.

They're very nice fellows. And one thing about this record that they made, this of Bish years, this PT4, this thing is sweeping the country. That's all they're playing around. New York. New York. And oh, it's a big hit over here and it is in England and it's really good in England, you know. And of course it wasn't the whole band. I think it was three or four of them.
Clarinet and the rhythm.

Clarinet and the rhythm, yeah, that's right. And they did a wonderful job. This thing is really, it's really going up to the top. And New York, when I got there, well, they sent them a letter in New York and they told them that, they thought by the time they get to the States that they would be the soul of a million. Because it had gone way over half a million, you know. And when I got to New York, that's all they played, was playing all day. All the radios, all the music shops, that's all they were playing. That number. And I say, well. Did you get to Ireland at all? No, we didn't get to Ireland. Where the ship stops at, that island to leave passengers off, the sea was so rough that they didn't stop there. They had to take those passengers into Liverpool and they had to go to Ireland by plane, either wait till day or so to go by this boat. What about France? Did you go through France at all? No, the band didn't go to France at all. And I didn't learn that I could have went to Paris in the morning and come back in the evening. I didn't know that until after we started to wake, you see. And that's one thing I was talking about Paris and they were, Miss Tate, I don't know, it looked like she was saying, well, we may go there. That's what she was telling me. I said, yeah. So I didn't know how far it was. And she was telling me about you could go on a boat and you'd have to, where this boat put you off in France, then you had to move to catch a train and come down to Paris, you see. So I get to talking to a fellow and I was telling him about Paris. He said, well, Joe, he said, well, I wish you had told me you wanted to go, he said, because he said, you can go in the morning and come back in the evening.
Yeah, pretty close.

Yeah. And I said, well, he said, yeah, he said, you don't take it no time, he said, to go to Paris from here, he said, go in the morning and come back in the evening. He said, if you had two or three days, he said, I'd take you and go on the boat train where they, on this boat, you can take your car, you know, and go on this ferry light. And then they go and leave you off, I think he said, he said, it's about a rhyme. Yeah. And he said, you keep naming the place where you come in, in France, he's saying you just drive down to Paris.
Did you get into Norway?
No, We just went to Sweden, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Scotland, and England.
Didn't get into Holland or Switzerland?
No, no, no. I stopped in Holland on the plane, but I mean, I didn't get off the plane. I got off the plane and I didn't see anything, but, you know, it's outside. Yeah, they, they, they.

The airport. Well, what it was, we had a chance to go to all those places, to Italy, France, Vienna, all those places we had a chance to go to after we got there. But trouble was, when they signed the contracts, they had made an arrangement for George to play three weeks with Kaye in Germany, you see. And after we got there, everybody wanted to book the band in these different places, you see. They wanted the band to play in Holland, Vienna, Italy, France, Austria, and Belgium. But by having them three weeks, George had to be there about a month before we could even went on this tour, you see. And then the fellows wasn't going to stay and pay the expense three or four weeks before they could go away. But everywhere that we played at, they actually was asked to return. And when we got to Sweden, they had three little young kids. One was 16, one was 17, and one was 21. And it was cold and ice on the ground and everything. And those kids were out there with just a banjo, a clarinet, and a soprano. And they was out there playing Dixieland, Welcome the Band to Sweden. Yeah. And those things really was touching. And we played another place in Denmark. I can't think of the name of the town right now. But anyway, we got there on a Sunday evening. This is about 7 o'clock. And the concert started at 8. And they had torches lit with, they had candles. They had these torches that looked like bulrushes, what we call them here. And so I was, they had so many of those torches. I took one of the torches with a candle, and the candles, grease got all over my overcoat. And those people went from the station. And they all walked in the middle street from the station to this hall, which was about four or five squares. And they had a jazz club there, and they made all of us honorary members of this jazz club. We all got, they gave us all pins. They gave George bouquets. And the people welcomed George Lewis so well. I mean, they gave him such a ovation, till he had to cry. He broke out of tears in this, in these places. And they all were fine. And this jazz, we went to another place. We played at the jazz club. Had a dinner for the band after the concert. And they all were young kids. They arranged, I say, from about 12 years old to about 24. All young, all young kids. And we all ate dinner. And from there we played one or two pieces. We had to leave, we had to get a train out and go back to Denmark. Then we were made honorary members of a club in England. And we played everywhere in England, I think that a band could go and play it. Because we, I don't know, we played so many places there. And everywhere we played at though, we had, we had tremendous crowds. And I think we played six concert in London. And all of those were really good crowds at all of the concert. And it was excellent because we didn't have a bad concert. And then playing behind Louis Armstrong within a week, a week or five days. And then Count Basie was playing three or four days behind us. So we was right in the middle of those two bands. But all the concerts was really good.
But your band went over better than any of them.

Well, everybody said that they thought that the band, we know that we had bigger crowds in Louis and many places. And everybody liked the band. They thought the band was better than Louis' band. They claimed that Louis made some changes in his band. Well, they played better together.
I mean, he's a big star, but sometimes his band isn't the greatest.

Yeah, well that's what they thought, but the most thing it was, I think it was because they said it was traditional. Yeah, they liked that. And they liked that, you see. And they really liked the band and all the fellas, they liked Jim, they liked everybody that was in the band. And everywhere we went at, we had a real welcome. And those fellas over there could tell me about musicians I didn't know anything about because they know that everybody played in Kit Thomas' band. And they called some fellas I didn't know. And they was telling me who was playing in bands years ago. They have all the pictures of all these bands that they have here. Every jazz book you can name, they have it. And they tell you all those things, and I say, well, it's a wonderful thing because I knew Buddy P.T., but I never did know, I think they say it's his father, somebody who played a trumpet, a trombone or something years ago. Joe P.T.
You didn't know him.
No, I didn't.
I didn't know him even, yeah.
Yeah, well, I was surprised. They had his picture there. And Buddy P.T., they knew all about Buddy P.T. and they have Mamie Smith. Oh, go ahead.
They knew something like Buddy P.T. and his stepfather and all?

Yeah, they know all those fellas and know all the members in Sam Morgan's band. And there was fellas that I had known very well and had forgot about and they were dead, you know? And I didn't think about it. And they called their names and it brought back memories. And we met a fella over there called Henrik in Denmark who traveled with the band and he was one of the swellest fellas you ever want to meet. Did bother you going down the wrong side of the street?
down the wrong side of the street.

Wrong side of the street. You know, it always looked like it was going to run into something and the car would be coming, it looked like it was heading into the car, you know. And a lot of times Jim would say, whoo, you know. It's quite a while to, you know, to get used to it. And it always looked like you're running into something, you're on the opposite side. And I never saw so many bicycles in my life as I saw in Denmark. They got some bicycles in Denmark. And it's amazing. And I'll tell you another thing that was on the trip that I noticed that it was amazing to see the people, how they have so much respect for the law. Now, in this way, of course, they got good and bad people everywhere you go. But the majority of the people over there, the police don't have any guns in England and Denmark and in Scotland and in Sweden. And when the police tell the people something, of course, they speak very nicely. They don't raise their voice. But when they say, now, look, sit and sit your thing. And it's that quick.
Yeah. And the people,

the people, actually, when they tell them something, they obey us. I mean, they don't, they say, now, all right, sit and sit your thing. You're out of order. And just that quick. It's okay. They'll, whatever they're doing, they'll quit doing it. The honest, the hardest trouble the police have with them is trying to hold them back for autographs. Now, they really, oh, they, they've autographs. they, they, just like somebody, like a bunch of hungry people trying to get something to eat. They, they, autographs, they, they write to the death. I never wrote my name so many times. I don't, I, and I don't think I ever will again unless I'd go back there. And they just keep you writing and they, they, they wait inside. They let so many in at the time after the concert. And you write, and you write, and write, and write. And then, the people, when it's time, they, they say, well, we can't sign anymore. And it hurts you to refuse people because they, they be asking you, please, please. A lot of them can't speak English, but they say, please write. Please, please write. Or you say, write here, write here, write here. And if you go to, write for one of them, they put so many in front of you to try, you can't see what you, what you're writing. And they really, they're staying out in the snow. That's what the thing that was, was so hurting when you'd have to refuse them. They'd be standing out in the snow and they'd wait out there two hours or something out there in that cold weather just to get you, you to write their name. And then when you get out there, they tell you, say, well, you can't sign no more. And they rush you in the car and they had the police and they get you in the car for you to get away. Because one thing about over there after 11 o'clock or 10 third at night, well, it's 11 o'clock, you can't find any place open to eat. So, a lot of times they'd be trying to get to places or either they would call up a place and ask them would he wait, would he stay open, say, 15 to 20 minutes. You know, and a lot of times they would say, yeah, and a lot of times they'd say, well, no, there's nobody here to fix anything at that time. The people are off. You understand? And a lot of times people would be kind enough that the cook or the waiter would stay a little over and wait there just to accommodate you.
How'd you like the food and the hotels and all over there?

Well, I tell you, the hotels over there are very nice and a lot of them are real modern. It's like the big hotels here and the only thing about the hotels over there, the people over there don't believe in too much heat. You know, that's one thing. It'd be cold out there and they have that heat on for a certain time and then they turn it off. You know, but you get used to that and some of them, well, they had some hotels who have heat continuously. Well, it's very similar. I mean, you run into those, but other than that, they have room and baths and everything looks like they have here. Now, some of the older hotels, they have what these WCs would, we might say community, I'd say, because you have to come outside and go down the hall to the bathroom or to the WC. they have two or three on the floor, but I mean, they're off a distance from your room. You see, you have to come out to go to them. How was the food
over there? How did you like it?

Well, the food was nice. I enjoyed the food because, and I say, it wasn't red beans and rice. We had that twice, but Joe cooked it. I think Joe cooked it in England. I know Joe cooked it. But other than that, the other food, you get chicken and fish and you have rice, liver, and they got a lot of places there where you can get this fine food. We ate in the Chinaman, the Salve, and we ate in a restaurant they called Simpson's Restaurant. And it's a modern restaurant. I mean, it's nothing in the States with no modern. And there were several of those. And I ate in one in Sweden, which was a real swell restaurant. And all the restaurants over there where I went to were most high-class restaurants because I went to several of them. Even went to two of them with a banjo player. And one was, he records for the London Decade. And then I went with a newspaper man from the Melody Lounge. And I went to the Omelette Bar. And I went to everything that you could see what was worthwhile in England and Scotland and in Denmark. Because I was interested in learning about these things. And I went to the palace. I saw the changes of the gods, the House of Parliament. I went to the, to the, to the, what they call the high court. I went to, I saw the king, the queen's palace where the queen lived at. I saw the big universities. Did you play
in any universities there?
No, we didn't play in the universities. All of it was theaters and, and, big halls and what, what they, what they call sports centers, you know.
Yeah.
They call sports centers like what we call the, we might call the, the auditorium. Yeah, like the, yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah,

New York. Yeah, I went to a prize fight over there. I saw Cooper in London. I saw them fight for the English heavyweight title. And they had some celebrities there. They had Bassett, the boy that fought last night. He was there. They introduced him, Norris, and this man that promoted the fight. I just remember his name, promoted the fight last night from California. He was there. And several other fighters. And the fighter who I wanted to see from Sweden was fighting Patterson. He was there and introduced him.
You didn't see him fight, though?

No, they just introduced him. And two or three days afterwards or so he was to fight Patterson. They had a plane of paper. Then I went and saw Madame Tussauds at Wax Museum. And they had a lady, her husband was a piano player. He was a piano player. His name is Graham. And his wife is named Molly. You know people. And she had taken me to all these places and she could explain the whole history of these things. I went to the Westminster. I went to St. Paul's Cathedral. And inside these churches they have different historical backgrounds. And she could explain all these things to me. It really was an enjoyable trip. I liked that. And then when we got to Sweden, to Denmark, they had a young man. He asked me had I been around. And I told him, no, I hadn't saw very much which places I had walked downtown. So he told me, he said, well, one day I'm going to come and get you. He said, well, it's available and I'm going to take you around. So I said, well, anytime it's convenient with you. So he said, well, I'll pick you up in about three days. He said, it was on a Tuesday. He said, I'll take you around. And I was supposed to go to Henrik's house to dinner. And so he said, well, I'll take you around and then I'll bring you to Henrik's. Henrik's knew him. And so sure enough he came, like he said, 12th day. And he brought me all over Copenhagen. And he showed me all the interesting things there. He brought me by this hospital where the, I think where there's Lisbon's, where they changed men into women. Oh yeah, I remember. And he brought me to this hospital and he brought me to this modern projects they have there. They have projects there, real modern projects. And he showed me those. Now there's one thing he was telling me that amazed me about these projects. One was 11 stewards. And he told me that 100 families got together and they built this. Not only one, they got several of them. There's seven of them. And they built that together and they moved in there. See these 100 families. And anything that these 100 families don't use, they rent it. See, so they bind this project together, 100 families. And I said, well that's really amazing, I say, that 100 families could buy a building like that and get along and live in it, you know. And it seems like it's very peaceful for what he told me, that they never have any incidents of any kind. And there's another thing that I wish that people throughout America could adopt this system. Now they got a system there like getting on streetcars. I don't care how, like if you're standing in a line, they got a line, they stand at this particular point. And I don't care how far a line is back when you see somebody coming up. They never try to get in front or nothing. They go back behind that line and they don't have no police there to make a way. And it'd be snowing or raining. And they all stand there and wait until their turn comes to get in those cars. Now sometimes it'd be three and four, five cars before the fellow behind the line can get in the car and he waits. And nobody pushes or nobody comes. See, like we, the people here got the system, they run and if you're waiting for the streetcar, they allow it to jump in front. You know, just come and jump right on in front. They never do that or no pushing or nothing. And I watched that in all those countries. And I used to stand them.
Just asking about your father in Chicago.

Oh yeah, well you see my father, at first he used to be a very good friend to Alphonse Mix. Alphonse Mix used to have the Tannery Club that was at Perdido and Drive. And him and my father were real good friends. Now he used to tell me about all the old musicians like Buddy Boland and Bab Frank and those people. And when I was about, I'd say about six or seven years old, my father brought me out to Lincoln Park. And they used to have a man, used to go up in a balloon. I think his name was Bartley, and Buddy Boland used to play back at this Lincoln Park. That used to be on the Sunday afternoon. But I never thought anything about no music or nothing like that. I just heard a band playing and it was playing. And I heard them say it was Buddy Boland and I heard them call that name. But I mean it wasn't nothing. I was too young to even know what he was playing or how he was playing or what. And after I'd grown up for a little bit, they had told me he had lost his mind because I used to hear my dad and them say that he lost his mind. But I never had heard him play. And Freddy Kepler, I didn't hear him play until I went to Chicago. I used to hear him talking about him when I went to Chicago and find out I heard him play, but I never did hear him play nothing in New Orleans.
stuff
I think it was November 23rd. He was 83.
Yeah, he was 83 years old. What instrument had he played?

Well he played trombone in a band, it was like a symphony band in Chicago, but it wasn't a band, what you would call a professional band, because this symphony band used to play in squares and things like that, but they used to play mostly, mostly were men who worked too, had other jobs.
Had he ever played down here?
No, he never played down here at all, because in fact he didn't learn the trombone until he went to Chicago.
When did he go, how old was he, or how old were you when he moved here?
My father went to Chicago when I was 16.
16, it was about 1916.
Yeah.
Was Professor John Robichaud your uncle, and that was your father's brother?
Yeah, it was my father's brother, that was my uncle.
And you remember him very well.

Oh yeah, I used to, well you see, he used to come to our house, sometimes he used to have rehearsal at the house, but that's quite small, he used to go to Franklin Street, and at 8 Franklin Franklin. Then he used to play all these different parties and dances and at restaurants like Antwine's, and all these hotels around here. Even he used to play the carnival balls here.
Well he played at Lincoln Park too I think, didn't he?

Yeah, he played Lincoln Park, St. Cathlin, and in the later days he played at the Larrick's Theatre, and he played at the Larrick's Theatre too, to the last of the Larrick's Theatre. When was that torn down?
I never saw it, I don't remember. Well, I couldn't tell you the… I mean about how old were you?

Exactly, oh well I was a man married when they tore that down, there was a two of that, the other down I was saying about 30, 32, I couldn't say exactly, but I know it was owned by Boudreaux, and… Did you ever play with your uncle? Sure, I played with my uncle on a boat, they used to have a boat go from this lake out here to Mandeville. Yeah, up and down!
Oh, some of these. Did you have your uncle John Robichaux in the Larrick's Theatre, did you play with him?

Yeah, well I played with him on a boat several times. Oh, it was on the lake. Yeah, on the lake, but Miss Margaret Kimball, she was a regular pianist in his band, and they had Kimball, the trumpet player, the wife and the husband playing in the band. So I played at her place, and he had a piano player once by the name of Buddy Christian, used to play for the moving pitches. I knew him, I knew him, he was in New York. Yeah, well I played at Buddy's place a lot of times for the movies, when my uncle played, when they had the band at the…
By the way, do you know if Buddy Christian is still living?
No, he's dead, I found out that he died. Yeah, that he died.
When Bunk's band was up in Georgia and all of them in New York in 1946, we saw him up at the Union.

I wondered if he still lived there. Yeah, well they told me he died. I asked about him, and they told me he was dead. Because he was a nice, a very nice fellow, and I knew him well. I knew him very well. And then the next thing about this theater business, so Ms. LaVoyne, Buddy left and went to New York, and they had a lady, her name was Ms. LaVoyne, and she was playing for Pitch of Sam, and they put an organ in there. And when they put this organ in there, well, she didn't know too much about the organ. And I think she said she had Professor Nixon teaching her to play the organ, her and Ms. Kimball, you know. And so I used to go around there, and finally I caught on how to play the organ, how to use the stops and things. And I used to play in her place, Ms. LaVoyne's place, and I played the organ. I had got very, very familiar with the organ, and I was doing real good with it. And finally when I started playing my, my own band, well, I started going out on the road when I heard again that they were going to tear it down and make a parking lot out of it.
Do you remember much about your uncle? He played violin, I understand. Anything else?

Yeah, he played bass drum in the brass bands. He was a left-handed, is that right? Left-handed violin player, and then he was a pretty good writer too. Yes, Mr. Very nice writer. In fact, I have a lot of his books here, what my aunt gave me, and music, they wanted to give me a lot of music, but I had, at that time I had more music than I could handle myself. So finally she gave something to different people, Peter Bocard and the library and most of it, to Dave Frank.
I believe somebody said, Kid Howard may have some of it, do you know?
Yeah. I forgot to ask him. Yeah, she gave Kid Howard some. Kid Howard had quite a bit too. And Dave Frank, he had a library and he had it that...
You know, I got one set of band books that Maurice Durand had, that had the John Robichaux's little rubber stamp printed in. I have those yet on there. Yeah, he has those.

Well, he had a whole lot of those. And there were some of those numbers that I'm sorry that I didn't take at that time, because you can't find them, and a lot of people look for them because they had a lot of things that they called mazookas, dance they used to do around here, and cakewalks, and they used to use special music for that, you know. Oh yeah. And there were tunes which right now you could do a whole lot with them.
The book I got was a brass band book, had my Maryland in it, and some of those pieces, and marches, it was all marches.
Yeah. Well, those are the things that I'm trying to get a hold of.
You want to look at my book sometime, it's not much in the way of mazookas or quadrilles, nothing like that.
Yeah, quadrilles too, that's another one.
I didn't get any of that.
Yeah.
But I do just have a few marches, I'll show you someday.
Yeah, well I appreciate it. And so anyway, after they disbanded the theater, my uncle he played around a while, but he got sick and he disbanded the band.
Do you remember when he died, the year?

No, I can't tell you the exact year off hand because I have it wrote down anyway, my cousins, they have it, but anyhow he died, I was out of town. I was out of town. And I went out of town, you see I came in and he was sick. Well he was right here at 611 Dauphin. And I went around and he was very, very little sick and I shaved him one day.

And I was living uptown and I came back two days after he was up and he had a few chickens and he was out there in the yard feeding the chickens and he was all right. And he had been very little sick and I didn't think that he was going to make it then. And so anyway, he got all right and he was up. So I went out of town because I used to go and see him, used to be down there four, sometimes five times a week. I used to come down and see him and sit down and talk. So finally when I left and went off this time, he was all right. I had been going in and out and coming in and he was all right. He was up and he was going around and everything. So when I went out the next time, there was a job jumped up. One of those, we say spare of a moment jobs, you know, it jumped up right away. It was a job that we got quick. So I had, I was an agent in Florida by the name of Brownie Roberts. He was out in Fort Lauderdale. Well he had wrote to me and he told me that he had about three weeks booking that he could give me right away if I could take it. So I told him, yeah, I said I could take it because I was playing at the rhythm club and the date I had there I could always get somebody to play at my place because I used to work out of that. So he said all right. So he told me it's where he wanted me to start. He wanted me to play Mobile and Pensacola and he wanted me to play Jacksonville, Fort Lauderdale, Tampa, St. Petersburg, and they had another, West Palm Beach. And so anyway, I told him that. So I went on down there and I didn't notify my aunt just where I would be at. So I went down there and when I come back he was dead and buried. They tried to find me. They were trying to find me and when they did, the day that they did find me, well I couldn't get back here on top.
Well it would be too late at that. So didn't Professor Oakeshore live uptown for a while on Camp Street?

Yeah, he used to live on Camp Street. Well he stayed on Camp Street practically all his life. He stayed up there until his wife died, see after his wife died, well that's where he moved downtown after that and then he remarried and remarried again. And then he remarried again, well then he stayed down here and then he sold the house up on Camp Street. Well they was living at 611 and he moved from 611, I believe he died there and then my aunt moved from 611 and she bought a house 920 Oysalon and that's where she was living there when she died. She's dead now too?
She's dead, yeah. No relatives except for nephews, people like you then I guess.
No, my aunt, she has two sisters.
Did John Robichaux have any children? Oh yeah, he had any of them living?
Yeah, he had two daughters, they're out in California. Well they're in California.
Yeah, they're out in California. They probably would remember a good deal about him too.
Yeah, yeah, well they write every night man.
Maybe if we got out there someday we could interview them, you know, for Tulane 2. Yeah, yeah. Get a little bit of back. Yeah, I guess they have it. Your uncle too.

Yeah, you see he, Uncle John he used to be away from home so much because a lot of times he had this, Larry's Theater, he used to stay in there a lot of times all night writing music. He used to be writing music all the time and the shows used to come in there without music and he used to write music for them and he'd write music for different people, for different bands and all that, and he was always writing. And he, I think he stayed up quite a bit writing in those shows he used to have to play a matinee every day too, you see. Oh yeah. And he used to play three shows a day.
He'd stay up all night and copy that music for the next day.

Yeah. A lot of times all he'd do was be able to go home and take a bath and he'd come back and a lot of times he used to be there because they had dressing rooms and showers and everything there in this theater.
Well by the way, do you have any good picture of him or his band, do you remember?
Well, I have a picture of him down by my cousin's house. I don't have any here myself and she has one picture of him down there.
I'd like to see it sometime. Maybe we could make a copy from it, you know. Yeah. Take a new negative and again. Yeah.
Well anytime, anytime you say so, I'll take you by the hand.
I would like to see it.
Yeah. Anytime. Yeah, he, uh, he was a very fine, fine man. I have to say that about him.
Well everybody has always said that.
Yeah, he, he had a swell reputation out here on everybody. And a good musician on top of that. He was a good musician.
A lot of people say he had the best band here for many years. For many years.

Yeah, he had the best band for many, many years. He had a real good band. And I'll tell you what I would, what I would like to get back to, uh, England again. For him. For, for. For one thing I wanted, I wanted to, you know, the musicians to know that how much these, these musicians over in Europe, not only England, are interested in the New Orleans music. And they actually, they, they have it at heart. And good as they play. Now we met some musicians, they actually play very, I mean they play really good. But they always feel like the New Orleans musicians are the greatest, you see. Because they tell you, they say, well we playing, we imitators and you are the originators. And we, we, we playing what you, what you play. But if you would just hear them play, you would just be saying, oh, these guys here is great, you know. But they, good as they play, they, they always, they feels that, uh, they, the imitators, you're the originators. And they say, well you're great, isn't it? Right. But they, that's the good. They got everything that you can name. They got good trumpet players. They got, uh, they got good clarinet players, trombone players, bass players. And to my surprise, I went in a place that had a Dixeland band there. This fellow was, I have his name in the book. But he had a singer with him. Her name was Barrow. And the place was so crowded, you know, I couldn't see the band when I first went in. And I heard this band playing and this band, you know, sound, oh, just like a New Orleans band, you know. And I say, oh, these guys really can play some music. And whoever it was, man. And then after a while I heard somebody singing the blues, you know, and it sounded like Mamie Smith or one of them. And when I look up there, it was a big blonde. Her name is Barrow. And then she can sing the blues and they got some boys over there who can play the blues just like they played years ago, you know, that real lowdown blues. Them guys can play those blues. I used to, I'd sit down and listen to them, I'd say, now look, these fellas can play these blues, but I wouldn't even think about knowing how to play them. You know, during those times it was for me and all of us used to play the blues was the first thing we was most alone, you know, a routine piano player. And those guys, man, play the blues and play you something, anything you want to play, and they got some progressive men over there too, or they got some of that, they got some of the blues and play everything you can name. And I met a guitar player, he was playing with Oscar Petterford, the bass player. Well in Germany, in Baden-Baden, on this television show, there was a play, you know, where we had been rehearsing, and they kept telling us they had a trio that was going to be on the show with us too, you see. So the last day of rehearsal, these guys came in, you know. But I didn't see them, I didn't see them when they come in because I had went to the canteen. And when I come back I heard a guitar player, I heard a guitar, this is a gun, you know, a guy was playing, and I said, this is a cat and you're playing this guitar, you know. And to George say, yeah man, who's this cat? And when we looked up there, this guy, he was playing and he was a guy, he was from Vienna.
Yeah.
Yeah. And man, he played some guitar. And this Oscar, they only had a drum, guitar, and they had Oscar.
Pettiford bass.
Pettiford bass. Yeah. He had been there for a couple of months and he had a terrible automobile accident.
I heard about him. Yeah.

It must have been terrible. He almost lost his tongue, but they sewed it back up and he's got six stitches in his forehead. And he said his eye was out and they put it back in, you know, and his sight is good and everything.
It makes you sick to read about this.

Yeah, I'm telling you, it really was an awful tragedy. And so anyway, he's getting along pretty good. He's getting along pretty good. And he said that the television show was the first wake he had since before Christmas. Well, I'm glad he was able to work with him. Yeah, he was able to work. And they had a tenor player with him, could play some tenor. And he wasn't on the show, but that's the group that he plays with. And this tenor player, he was terrific. Then I met Stan Getz. He lives in. Did he open there? Yeah, he lives there. He made his home in Copenhagen. And I met a trumpet there. And I met a, he's married, got a wife and got kids and that's where he's living at. And he just goes from, whenever he goes out to play he leaves, you know. And I met a trumpet player over there called Bailey. He used to play with Lyle and Hampton. He's living in Sweden now. Yeah. And you see he left, he's been, he'd have made his home in Sweden now. And he, oh, he's a terrific trumpet player. He came and played where he was playing at one night. And he plays pretty good. Then I met a piano player out of New York they called Heinz. Heinz, a Heimer. He was kind of tall boy, he was a white boy, but he played up some piano. And I told him all about Batura and Schalke. I told him Schalke is the, it's just about the oldest Dixon and trumpet player we have now. I mean, from the fellas back, you know. Yeah, he was a little bit of a town. Yeah, and I told him, you know, what a good man he was. And a lot of fellas knew of him that had been here, but the others didn't, you know.
Some people tell me at times that Schalke plays a lot, or one time played a lot like Kid Rene, too.

Well, yeah, I'll tell you one thing about it, if the people never pay much attention, Schalke is asking one of the original Dixon and trumpet men. I mean, he's one of them real, real, what you call Dixon and trumpet men. You know what I'm saying? You know what I'm saying? We got a lot of fellas that play a lot of horn and play it loud, but I mean when you come down to the street, talk about the original, that's it. Schalke is actually that kind of a trumpet player. You can't get that away from him, man. He's a good trumpet player.
Speaking of trumpet players, I was going to ask you about Tick Chambers because I never knew anything about him.
He was another good trumpet player. Now that was another trumpet player that you don't hear much about.
He never made any records, so nobody knows about him.

He never made any records, but he was a good trumpet player, and he was quite popular around New Orleans, too, before he left, went to Chicago. Him and Tick Chambers both. Tick Chambers, I meant to say, Jimmy Strokes was another good trumpet player he was from New Orleans.
So how did Tick get played? Was he a high note man?

No, I'll tell you, he played on a style like Buddy P.T., right? On a style like Schalke played, he was that kind of trumpet player. A real nice trumpet player. And he stayed around Chicago, he stayed around Chicago and died. He left here and never did come back. Never came back. Never did come back to New Orleans anymore. Just like my uncle, both of my uncles, Johnny Dodds, he left and his uncle through second marriage.
I was going to ask you how they were related. Baby once mentioned something about it, too. I didn't know just how you were related.

Yeah, well, see, they're the oldest brother, Willie. They married, he married my mother. After my father and mother separated. He married my mother and that was his second marriage and that's how we got to, you know, his uncle through marriage.
He was so mad.
But I was, I was.

around there before either one of them know how to play. I didn't know how to play anything, I wasn't thinking about music and they wasn't playing anything so finally Baby wanted to learn drums and the father brought them a drum. They was living over in Waverly, Mississippi. In fact that's where they were born, you know everybody says it's New Orleans, but they were born in Waverly, Mississippi, a little town, about six miles. So then Baby started playing the drum and then Johnny got the clarinet and he used to practice and he used to sit out on the gutter coils and practice. And so finally he got the playing and he got in the band, and he hired him and he needed a clarinet player and he played with Ori and then he played around Spanos or someplace they called him little hunky-ton. Yeah. And then from there Joe Oliver, he was playing in the Orange Band and Joe Oliver went to Chicago and Joe Oliver sent for him and he went to Chicago and he'd never been back here since.
You knew that Baby died a month ago.

Yeah, I didn't know it until we had to pick up a magazine over there and they had it in his magazine that he had to pass. And the people over there, you know, it was kind of shocked to them. Yeah, of course he'd been so sick since September.
He'd been...

Because they had been asking me about it and I told them that he was a little sick because the time that you told me you had went up there. Yeah. Yeah, well after my father's death when I went up there, he was sick but he was at home, you know.
Yeah, he'd been in the hospital.
Yeah, he'd been in the hospital, yeah. So I told him, I said, well Baby was very little sick. I said, I don't think he's going to make it. Well Johnny, Johnny's got a son here.
Well that's right, I haven't seen him since I've been there.
Rudolph, I think. Yeah, well he drives a cab on the Morrison cab line. Then he's got a nephew there which is... Oh Lawrence Dent, I know him.
Lawrence Dent, yeah. I know him, I see him, he plays in one of the bands, the Gibson band. Is that good clarinet now?

Yeah, that's what Lawrence said. So I told Lawrence, Christmas evening, the night I was leaving, he brought me here. He brought me home because I had to get ready to go to the station. And I told him about Baby being sick and he said that he was thinking he was going to go to Chicago. I said, well he's very little sick. I said, now I wrote him a card and I got an answer from him. I said, but he's very, very little. And so I said, he said, well I'm going to drive up there and see about him. Now I don't know if he went. You see, and after I got... Yeah, so I wrote to him from England and somebody answered the letter, you know, he was very bad off. He was expecting him and so when I pick up this magazine he had them passed. All three of them, all three of the brothers died in Chicago.
The Baby lived longer to be older than any of them and also older than any of his sisters too.
That's right. Everybody died. The first one died. He had a sister named Hattie. She died. Then his sister Rosa died. Then his older brother Willie died. Then Johnny died. He was the last one.
Johnny was just 48 when he died and Baby made 64.
64, yeah.
And you know Johnny never did drink and Johnny was very... Oh, sorry, took care of himself.

Yeah, yeah. Johnny was a fella he didn't dissipate any too much. A lot of people thought he was self conceited. But Johnny was a very fine fella. He was just a fine man but he didn't even stand up all night drinking and waking all day. Yeah. I mean drinking all day. When he'd get off from wake he might spend half an hour or something like that but he was gone he'd go home. You see? But Johnny was very good. But Baby would stay up all day.
Oh yeah, Baby would stay up all day.

He could take care of himself at all and yet he'd... Baby liked to drink the last time. He outlived him. Yeah, when we played at the Hunt Club he came out there and you know he could hardly hold the sticks and he was trying to play the drum. You know we played something slow. I mean he kind of made out for a man with a stroke you see. And still he was drinking then.
He wasn't supposed to drink then?

Wasn't supposed to drink. And when we brought him home he wants to get a drink and I begged him and I said, Baby, you ain't got no business drinking. I said, man, come on, let's go home. And he just said he kept a warning and said he wanted to see a friend and he stopped there and he wanted to see a friend. He bought a drink and he had to go upstairs where he lived at. And I got out there and bought him home and told me he's alright, he couldn't make it home, he couldn't make it upstairs and everything. Well finally he went up there upstairs, alright and everything.
He took care of himself.
But I don't think that was doing him any good.
No, no I don't believe so.
Well I think he probably would have lasted a little longer if he had been taking care of himself.
You never know though, like he said Johnny took care of himself and he didn't.

Yeah, well you know people have that saying, if a fellow don't drink or don't smoke and he dies, the guy who the doctor tell him that he shouldn't drink, he'll tell you say, well, since the one never did drink and he died, you understand, so look at me, I'm still living and I'll drink. And eventually he might last a little longer, you know. That's right. So he just, so that's one thing I, I do recommend the boys who play Dixieland to keep it up, play the noise, because if they don't, just like I said in England in the interview, for us to hear jazz, we're going to have to go over there if we just keep it up, because all the youngsters over there, that's all they're doing. That's the majority. The kids don't take it up. The kids don't take it up. The little kids over there, ten, twelve years old, is playing jazz. That's young. That's young, that's right. Playing jazz. And them at sixteen is playing bands, they got bands. Even the school, we played a place in, yeah it was in Sweden. We played in Sweden, when the concert was over they had a school band who came there on the bus, you know, just like these college bands here. Played all the Dixieland tunes and all the spirituals and things. Out there in that snow playing it when we, after we, celebrating us after we came out the concert, after the concert was over. And I said now let's see how we are letting the things back, what they are, they calls it art. They love it.
Well this tape is just about out, do you feel like talking a little longer? I was going to ask about some of those early piano players, like Game Kid again, what style he played?

Well I tell you Game Kid was a blues piano player and he played a couple of rags, you know, he played some rags too. And he was a very famous piano player uptown during the time when I was a kid, you know. And then after.
Do you know where he came from? Was he from here or?
Yeah, I'm sure he was from here. So far as I could learn about it, he's a piano player from here and he came from out front of town. He came out of the Irish Channel. And then they had the.
Did he read or did he just pick it up himself?

No. He wasn't a reader, he just picked it up himself. Did he play in bands or by himself? Yeah, he played by himself. Most of them he played was parties and fish fries and around these hunky tunks. Yeah. That's the kind of piano player he was. But he played a lot of parties and a lot of fish fries things, that's why he was doing that for a living.
Do you know if he ever composed any pieces, any certain ones that he made up or something

that you remember? Yeah, he composed a couple of pieces because they used to, he had a number, they used to call it Game Kid and he used to play that and they used to have a blues. The blues, they played the blues, they used to call it the kids. They used to call it the kids and he used to play those blues, those two pieces that I know that he composed himself.
About how old a man was he? Well as they say when you were ten years old, how old was he grown or just a few years

older? No, he was about twenty, twenty-four years old. When you were ten? Yeah, he was about twenty-four then. I know he was quite a young man. He was around the age with a piano player I know they called Oscar Desdune.
Oscar Desdune?
Yeah, Oscar Desdune. He used to play piano when he was a reader.

Is that the same name? There was a trombone player, but that name used to work with little brother Montgomery. Uh. In Jelly Roll played a blues called Mamie's Blues, Mamie Desdune. Was there any relation to them? Mamie Desdune.

I tell you, I've been trying to find out, I've been asking different fellows, these old fellows about this Mamie Desdune since I got this book of Jelly Rolls, you know. And I was reading about it and I've been asking fellows about it and it seems like they don't recall her, you know, fellows who used to be in Storyville during that time.
Yeah, Bunk Johnson, of course he was much older than we are, he talked about her a little bit, but I don't know much about her either.
