Yeah, well the piano players that I actually know, they were older than me, but the answer ones that I know who played back in Storyville during those times was Fred Washington, which was a great piano player.
You know, we got to see him when Professor Renette and I went out to California. Yeah. And he's paralyzed now too. Oh yeah? Yeah, his wife has to dress him.
Oh.
He can't do a thing for himself. Any little thing he has to do, she has to feed him. Oh.

Everything he does. Well he was a great piano player, he was, that's who Steve Lewis adopted his style from Fred Washington. Fred Washington was a great piano player and I'll tell you another piano player who was really good, when I say the great piano player because the different chords that the fellows are making now called modern chords, what Fred Washington was making in those days. He was, that's the kind of piano he was playing.
I believe what you told me once is when he was around nobody else would play. Yeah.

The jelly roll on and we'd have to get on. Oh yeah, the jelly roll, and I couldn't hold a life for Fred Washington. Fred Washington was playing and then they had another jazz piano player that nobody, I don't mean I never read no books or nothing on him and he was absolutely good. It was a piano player called Lewis Wade. Well I've heard the name. Yeah, he was one of the jazz piano players he could play.
He played bands too?

Yeah, he played bands and played for shows and everything but he didn't read. But he was a good piano man, he could play. Now he was a piano player that you didn't hear much about. Then there's a piano player they called Albert Cowell.
Oh I've heard of him.

Yeah, he was a great piano player. They had another piano player they called Nune. He was some kin to the Caillus. Yeah, he was a good piano player. They had the Red Caillou. What was here he was very good. Red Caillou. Yeah, he went to California, he died in California, in Oakland. He was a very good piano player. Of course Red Caillou was around my age, Red Caillou. Then they had another piano player here, what was a good piano player, Summersler Rouse. Now he, well see Summersler Rouse he was a good piano player. And then he was the only piano player that, out of all the good piano players that I know could play this much piano in B natural as the Irish piano player could play in F or C. See he could, the keys that he played in was F sharp, B natural and E natural. Those was the keys that he played in. Now the E is the keys, he couldn't play in them. He was a routine player. He was fine. Yeah, but he was good, he was a really good piano player. He died and had Big Eye Louis, he was from uptown, he was a piano player too. Not Big Eye Louis Nelson, the client of that player, there's another Big Eye Louis.
I didn't really know about him.

Yeah, he was a good, he was a very wonderful piano player. I finally think his last name was Robert, Louis Robertson. Everybody called him Big Eye Louis. He was a good piano player. Another piano player was very good in his younger days, in his old days, naturally he kind of slowed up a little bit. But that was his son, his trumpet player Newman. Newman. Newman? Yeah. See the trumpet player Newman, Newman was around there, he played with Camp Basie.
Oh sure, yeah.
Yeah, well his father. His father was a wonderful piano player. Yeah, his father was a good piano player. And he finally, I think the last band he played with was with Peter Bocas, remember?
The Creole.
The Creole. Serenaders.
That's right.
That's right.
I don't know about him. We talked to Peter, I don't think Peter told us anything about him.
Peter wasn't thinking because that's the last band he played with. When Peter never had a Creole serenade, he was a piano player.
Might have mentioned him, but he was really good then.
Yeah, he was really good piano player, nice musician too. Yeah, he was good and in his younger days he was really good piano player.
Did you know Alfred Wilson? Did you mention him?
Alfred Wilson.
He used to play in the district I think at Countess Willie Piazza's house.
Alfred Wilson? I know you though Wilson.
No, he was from Kansas City. Kansas City, yeah, he was good. He came from Algiers or something.

Professor Minetta told us about a fellow that stayed on the other side of the river. He said he was really wonderful, Gusty O'Neal. Did you ever hear him?
Yeah, I know him. Yeah, he was good too.
Did you like him too?

Yeah, yeah, yeah, he was a good piano player. O'Neal was a good piano player. And also there was another piano player, oh he played nice piano too, and he was playing in the district during the time when ... Did you ever hear Tony Jackson? Oh, Tony Jackson. He was good. Yeah, I heard Tony Jackson, Louis Wade, Fred Washington, and I'm trying to think of this other piano player. I heard them all three playing in a house at one time, you know, one take time. Yeah. And he was a very good piano player. And then the next time I heard him was in Chicago, he used to play at the E-Light when I went up to Chicago.
Some people have told me he was a wonderful pianist, and others say well he was mostly a good singer and entertainer. Was he a wonderful pianist?

No, he was a wonderful piano player, you see. People say that, you see, because he was an entertainer and he could be talking and holding a conversation and talk to anybody and just go ahead and play what he was playing and he never missed a note and just be talking about anything and don't look at the piano. But some people say oh he was a good entertainer, but he was a good piano player, period. Yeah. Yeah, he was a good piano player.
He wrote a lot of good numbers too, like Play Baby and ...
Yeah, yeah, he actually was a good piano player. And they had Arthur Campbell too.
Oh yes. I don't know him, but I mean ...
Yeah, he was a nice piano player. He went to Chicago, I think he died in Chicago too.
He made one record with Freddie Keppert.

That's right. He was on that record too. That's right, Arthur Campbell. And he was a good piano player. Now these fellas would play piano during those times. They had so many of them that I could name, but they wasn't the really top piano players. Well they used to, I don't know if it was his cousin or what, but they used to live at Thood and Clara. And all the bands used to be on the wagon, used to stop and go in their house, and on Sundays they used to have jam sessions there all the time. The Shields? The Shields, yeah. And they had a piano player used to go there, out their house and play all the time. His name was, his name was Willis. His name was Willis. He was a very good piano player and he moved, he left here and went to California and he died. And Steve Lewis and this Shields, his cousin or brothers, he was playing in Storyville at that time.
Well there's another white pianist I've heard of, Kid Ross I believe. Did you know him? No. I think he played at Lula White's house for a while.
No I didn't know him. I know Lula White's nephew.
Spencer?
Spencer Williams, yeah. I know him. I saw him in New York too.

Yeah, he's living over there but he comes to the states every year, sometimes twice a year. And I happened to see him by Mills on Broadway, Broadway 49.
Another pianist, when you were talking about Galveston and that part of Texas, did you ever run into Lazy Daddy over there? Yeah. Fillmore I guess. Yeah, yeah. How was he?

I never got to know him. But he was a good piano player, yeah, he was good. I know him and I know a fellow called Jimmy Prye, he was another pretty good piano player around that way. And there's another piano player who is living the day, was a very famous piano player among all the piano players because they used to go sit in the show to listen at him play. They used to listen to the guys that didn't read, used to listen at him to catch tunes for him. I mean he was a piano player with use of a lot of harmony and that was McNamara. Yeah, he plays, I think he's on, I think he plays with this band WDSU. He played organ too. He used to play, he used to play the organ at the Lowest State and then he played piano. His name, Mac Mamamara I think his name is. Yeah. He's very, very, of course if you hear him now you can tell he used to get piano right today, but he was good then. I think he played with this Don Busters.
Oh yeah.
Yeah, he used to play with, when Al Huyte was playing with him.
A couple of other fellas that maybe they were, left Chicago, I mean they went up to Chicago and different places before you were grown. Richard M. Jones, Mione Jones, did you ever hear him?
Oh I know it, Mione Jones, before he left here and then when I went to Chicago I met him and we used to be around Clarence Williams when Clarence Williams had the music store. I know it.
Both of those men, they wrote a lot of pieces but were they really first rate pianists? I couldn't tell from the record.
I'll tell you, Mione Jones wasn't a very good piano player and then Clarence Williams wasn't what you call a good piano player.
I didn't think so either from the records.

They wrote a lot of good composers. No, they wrote a lot of good tunes and they had another one that used to be with him, George Jones, he played piano. He wasn't much of a piano player. Well he wrote a couple of tunes with Williams and he was up there with Williams when they had two music stores. They had one at 30 Foison State, one at 47 and they stayed there and finally they went to New York. And Clarence Williams, Foison used to play drum around here, then he started playing piano and he's a comedian. Then he had a show, he opened up a show called The Rosebud up on Dry Snail Phillip.
Oh yeah, Professor Minetta said he had played up there once.

Yeah, and Bichet, that's the first time I heard Bichet play, Bichet was working for Clarence. And then he had hired a woman to play piano for the show, her name was Emily, Emily Hines I think it was. She played piano for the show and he was the comedian on the show on the stage.
Yeah.

And I used to be up there every day and be at the rehearsals and he had Sweetie Matthews working with him, Octavia Summers, and they had Bichet and that was actually the first saxophone that Bichet ever played was Clarence Williams' saxophone.
Was it an alto or a C melody?

It was a, I'm pretty sure it was a C melody, either alto, but I think it was a C melody. Because anyway, they was on advertisement and Clarence was playing this saxophone and Bichet was playing the clarinet and they had a piano and a wagon and they had the drum. And it was on advertisement and I was on the wagon with them and Bichet was saying he bet he could learn how to play that thing, you know. And so he was fooling around with it and fooling around with it and he blowed a couple of good notes on it and so Clarence told him, he said, well if you think you can learn it, he said, I'm going to let you take it home with you. He said, no. He said, I'm telling you. He said, I don't want you to pawn my home. That's what the Clarence told Bichet. And Bichet said, no, I'm going to bring it, I'm learning. So he come up there that next day and you know he fooled around and he learned how to play a number on it, you know. And so then Clarence Williams let him use the horn and when you find around he could play it better than Clarence, you know. And then Bichet left and went to Chicago and the next time I heard him, he was playing the soprano. He was playing the soprano. He was playing the soprano. So I said, well you know, he was very apt. He learned something right quick. Because he learned how to play that horn so quick and during that time when Clarence had the saxophone, had his saxophone rather, there was a very few saxophones in the city. And if I'm not mistaken, it was between him and Charlie McQuirtus who was the first color that had ever had a saxophone. And there was a very few in the city at all among white-up colored saxophones. And Bichet learned how to play it right now. In a week's time he was playing the double out that C melody. I think it was C melody.

I wanted to ask, before I forget it, something about those records you made. First of all, the Lee Collins records with Jones, which you made with Dave Jones too. Did you play with the band all the time at the end? Oh yeah.

I played with the band regularly. I played at the, the band used to play at this club right here where the post office is on Bienville. It was named the, I call it the club not so long ago we used to talk. Well anyway we were.
Not the one down with the river, but was that it down with the river?
